summary:
El Salvador presents a specific and documented risk profile for trans visitors. The country has no Gender Identity Law and no legal recognition of gender identity, so trans visitors have no domestic mechanism to correct or align documents with their gender. The penal code does contain an enhanced penalty for bias-motivated killing: in September 2015 the National Assembly approved reforms under which homicides motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender carry 30 to 60 years under Article 129.

The limits of that framework are illustrated by the killing of Camila Díaz Córdova, a trans Salvadoran woman who had been deported from the United States and was killed in January 2019. In July 2020 a San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of her murder and sentenced each to 20 years. The judgment was the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person, and Human Rights Watch treated it as significant for transgender Salvadorans' rights while documenting that violence and discrimination against LGBT people continued.

Human Rights Watch reports of October 2020 and January 2021 record that El Salvador, with Guatemala and Honduras, fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, and that the resulting insecurity drives asylum claims to the United States. The reports document concrete obstacles victims encounter when attempting to obtain police and judicial protection.

The peer-reviewed record on the lethal violence is longitudinal: a 2024 study in the journal Dilemas, produced at Fundação Oswaldo Cruz, profiles the crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000 to 2020, giving the documented baseline for anti-LGBTI+ killings in the country over two decades.

Since the state of exception began in March 2022, trans women have been among those swept up in mass raids and held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. A February 2024 investigation by GatoEncerrado records the case of Jennifer, arrested in San Salvador on 14 April 2022 and held first at the El Penalito police lockups and then in prison. Custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out along with another trans woman named Rosa for outdoor punishment drills while handcuffed and forced to squat in the sun, and denied her access to the HIV clinic. A judge freed her after roughly four months, finding that her arrest had no basis; Rosa remained imprisoned at the time of reporting.

Socorro Jurídico Humanista and Cristosal link this treatment to the absence of a Gender Identity Law. The prison system assigns placement by birth sex, contains no special custody provision for trans detainees, and trans detainees are exposed to targeted abuse inside it, with no effective recourse while the state of exception runs.
tangentialFactors:
The regional picture matters for expectation-setting. Human Rights Watch groups El Salvador with Guatemala and Honduras as three neighbouring countries where violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people go inadequately addressed, and where the failures of police and judicial protection push LGBT Salvadorans, Guatemalans and Hondurans into asylum claims in the United States.

A tension runs through the evidence base. The 2015 Article 129 reforms and the 2020 Díaz Córdova conviction show that the legal machinery for prosecuting bias-motivated killing exists and has been used at least once against police officers, while the same period produced the HRW findings of entrenched discrimination, documented obstacles to obtaining protection, and the 2024 GatoEncerrado account of abuse inside the prison system by state custodians.

The security framework operating since March 2022 changes the exposure calculus for gender-nonconforming people. Whatever the effect of the crackdown on other forms of street crime, the documented mechanism in this inventory is detention: trans women are captured in mass raids, held without any gender-identity accommodation, and subjected to abuse that a judge later found had no lawful basis.
localsOnly:
Residents live without any form of legal gender recognition. No Gender Identity Law exists, so Salvadorans cannot obtain documents matching their gender, and the prison system continues to place people by birth sex.

The absence of a Gender Identity Law is treated by Socorro Jurídico Humanista, Cristosal and other organisations as the structural cause of the abuse documented inside the prison system, and trans Salvadorans detained under the state of exception remain exposed to forced shaving, punitive drill, isolation and denial of medical care, including HIV treatment.

Discrimination and violence have been persistent enough over the 2000 to 2020 period to sustain regular outward migration and asylum claims, and Salvadoran LGBT people continue to cite obstacles to obtaining police and judicial protection as a reason for leaving.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether Article 129's enhanced penalties have been applied to any trans victim other than Camila Díaz Córdova, and how often the provision is charged in practice.

Unresolved: the status of Rosa after February 2024, when the GatoEncerrado report recorded her still imprisoned; no later reporting is provided.

Not sourced here: entry and visa rules for El Salvador, border or airport screening practices, any document gender-marker requirement applied at entry, or the treatment of foreign gender markers by Salvadoran authorities. The dossier carries no finding on these points from the present inventory.

Not sourced here: whether the state of exception remains in force beyond early 2024, the current national homicide rate, and any provision on marriage or partner recognition for transgender visitors or residents.
